_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: Since it is in the heart: the essence of his prohibition depends on the wickedness of his heart, that he knew Whom he blasphemed; therefore it is not considered an action. But with bowing, we see him bowing to an idol.
rashi:a1.2: Marginal gloss: Since it is in the heart: the essence of his prohibition lies in the thought of the heart, and there is no action here; what he speaks only voices his prohibition. But the bending of one’s height is the essence of that prohibition [bowing], for were he speaking of one who accepts an idol [as a god] without bowing, he would not be liable [on that count]; the essence there is not in the heart, rather the bending is what makes him liable. So it seems to me.
rashi:a2.1: Conspiring witnesses are excluded: in Torat Kohanim, regarding the bull of the anointed priest. This is what it says there: After we have included matters that concern idol worship and matters that do not concern idol worship, I might think I include the inciter, the one who leads [a town] astray, and conspiring witnesses. The verse states “and does” [Leviticus 4:2]: those in which there is no action are excluded. They are excluded from the category of the sin offering.
rashi:a2.2: But “at the mouth” is written regarding them: so let us say the twisting of their mouth is an action.
rashi:a2.3: Since they are through sight: the essence of their testimony is what the eye saw, since they testify to what they saw; therefore it is not considered an action.
rashi:a3.1: Liable for each and every one: lashes, if he ate them after a single forewarning.
rashi:a4.1: One is flogged for a general prohibition: for each and every one [of the things it includes].
rashi:a4.2: And the Rabbis hold one is not flogged: and if you ask, then let him not be flogged even once? He is at least flogged once.
rashi:a8.1: And derive “ox” “ox” from Shabbat: “That your ox may rest” (Exodus 23:12). Just as there, undomesticated animals and birds are like it, as we establish in Bava Kamma, in the chapter Shor SheNagaḥ et HaPara (Bava Kamma 54b; see there). [Rashi’s text reads the analogy from Shabbat, where the daf reads Sinai.]
rashi:a10.1: All fat of sheep: for now there is no verbal analogy [as “sheep” is not written regarding Shabbat].
rashi:a13.1: An ox has an increase in libations: “Half a hin shall be for the bull.”
rashi:a15.1: A goat has an increase regarding idol worship: for an individual.
rashi:a16.1: One from two: from the feature common to them, that they are a species of domesticated animal, their fat is forbidden, and the sacrificial portions of their firstborn are offered.
rashi:a17.1: They have an increase regarding idol worship: a bull for the community and a goat for an individual.
rashi:a18.1: This is the reading: “What about an ox and a sheep? They have an increase at the altar”: an ox in libations and a sheep in its tail; but a goat has no increase at the altar in its offering.
rashi:a20.1: But when the verse is written, it is written in the context of sacrificial animals: as it is written (Leviticus 7[:25]), “For whoever eats the fat of the animal…”. Since it is written in the context of sacrificial animals, undomesticated animals certainly do not apply there; therefore “ox and sheep” is not needed to permit undomesticated animals.
rashi:a21.1: By inference the Rabbis hold: that we do not derive the prohibition of “all fat” from its context? [Said] in astonishment.
rashi:a21.2: Everyone derives a matter learned from its context: in general. But here it is not its context, since this one is a prohibition and that one is karet.
rashi:a21.3: And here they disagree about this, etc.: the reading written in the books here is corrupt, the work of mistaken commentators who were not expert in the passage and wrote their garbled explanation into the text. The arrangement is this and no more: “And here they disagree about this: one Sage holds we derive a prohibition from a prohibition and a prohibition from karet, and the other Sage holds we derive a prohibition from a prohibition but do not derive a prohibition from karet.” And this is its explanation: Rabbi Yishmael holds we derive a matter from its context, whether a prohibition from a prohibition or a prohibition from karet.
rashi:a24.1: And the Rabbis hold: a prohibition from a prohibition, we derive one from the other when they are in one passage, as a matter learned from its context, like the case of meat in milk taught in the chapter Kol HaBasar (Ḥullin 115b): “You shall not eat it”: the verse speaks of meat in milk. But a prohibition from karet, as here, we do not derive as a matter learned from its context. Therefore, had “ox and sheep and goat” not been written, I would have said undomesticated animals are included.
rashi:a25.1: And if you wish, say the reason of the Rabbis: is that they need this “ox and sheep and goat” for the teaching of Rav Mari.
rashi:a25.2: The tail of a non-sacred animal should be prohibited: since it is called fat, in the chapter Kol HaBasar (Ḥullin 117a).
rashi:a25.3: That is equal in all three: that is called fat in all three; and the tail is called fat only in a sheep.
rashi:a26.1: If so, let it write “all fat of ox and sheep”: and from there I would exclude the tail, since we require something equal in both of them.
rashi:a27.1: The prohibition of forbidden relations: he mentions forbidden relations because there are many cases there, with a prohibition for each one.
rashi:a28.1: “From one of them” [me’aḥat mehena]: implies that for one he is liable; “them,” several sin offerings.
rashi:a29.1: Fat and fat: two olive-bulks of fat.
rashi:a29.2: One name: the fat of the kidneys, or the fat of the intestines, is one name. We do not read “in one lapse of awareness” [here].
rashi:a29.3: Two names: an olive-bulk from upon the kidney and an olive-bulk from upon the intestines.
rashi:a30.1: Since lapses of awareness separate: since he became aware in between, these are two errors, and the Merciful One made the sin offering depend on awareness, as it is written (Leviticus 4[:23]): “Or if his sin be made known to him.”
rashi:a31.1: Fat of notar: as there are two errors involving two karet prohibitions, fat and notar, and he is liable to two sin offerings.
rashi:a31.2: Let him be liable on account of the sacred as well: a guilt offering for misuse [of consecrated property].
rashi:a32.1: Rather, Rav Sheshet said: for example, where he ate fat of the sacred: and in fact it is on account of fat that he is liable to two; that is why the guilt offering for misuse is not counted, only [the sin offerings] of one name. And it is Rabbi Yehuda, who renders one liable to two for the fat of consecrated animals on account of fat; and the “two names” it teaches are because two verses are written concerning the fat of consecrated animals.
rashi:a32.2: Fat of a carcass, he is flogged two: on account of fat and on account of a carcass. And [fat of] consecrated animals: on account of fat and on account of a non-priest [eating sacred food].
rashi:a32.3: Three: two on account of fat, as is explained below, and one on account of a non-priest.
rashi:a33.1: And let us establish: the baraita above, which teaches “two names,” that is, from two animals of two species, as Rabbi Yishmael.
tosafot:a2.1: Since they are through sight: This is puzzling: how does this answer the inciter and the one who leads astray [whom the same baraita excludes]? Rabbeinu Nissim answered in Megillat Setarim: since the blasphemer is “in the heart,” all of those are likewise; but conspiring witnesses, who are not “in the heart,” needed the answer that they are “through sight.” And in his book he wrote [the reading]: “Conspiring witnesses, since they are [subject to] ‘if’,” meaning “if he does not tell” [Leviticus 5:1]; and it is explained in the chapter Shevuat HaEdut that they become liable only in court. Therefore they are not liable through the twisting of the lips, for if so, they would be liable even outside court; their telling alone, that is, their mouth, does not bring the liability. But elsewhere, where one is liable through his speech alone, the twisting of his lips is an action.
tosafot:a5.1: Why do I need “ox and sheep and goat”? Learn from it to separate: This is puzzling: why are three needed to separate? One would suffice.
gershom:a1.1: [A printer’s note: “Up to here belongs to 3b.”] Rava said: The blasphemer is different, since the essence of his prohibition is the thought of the heart, and thought is not an action. But elsewhere, where we do not go after thought, we say that the twisting of his lips is an action.
gershom:a2.1: Rabbi Zeira raises an objection: “Conspiring witnesses are excluded.” This is a baraita in Torat Kohanim, which teaches: Or, just as idol worship is something for which one is liable to court-imposed death, so too I include only what carries court-imposed death. What do I include? For example, one who curses his father or mother, the inciter, the one who leads astray, [the false] prophet, and conspiring witnesses. The verse states “and does”: those in which there is no action are excluded; therefore they have no sin offering.
gershom:a3.1: But why: is there no action in them? Regarding witnesses “at the mouth” is written: “At the mouth of two witnesses.” Let us say the twisting of the lip is an action, and they should be liable to a sin offering.
gershom:a4.1: Rava said: Conspiring witnesses are different, since they are [primarily] through sight: the essence of their testimony is that they testify “we saw such-and-such,” and in seeing there is no action. That is why their unwitting sin was not given atonement [by an offering], since there is no action in it.
gershom:a5.1: To render one liable for each and every one: for each and every species.
gershom:a6.1: [An editor’s note: it seems one should read “One is flogged for a general prohibition, and this is a prohibition, etc.”] That is a general prohibition, which includes the fat of ox, sheep and goat.
gershom:a7.1: And the Rabbis hold one is not flogged: but he is flogged at least once.
gershom:a8.1: Since the verses are superfluous: [they come] to separate; for let the verse write “You shall eat no fat,” and all would be included.
gershom:a9.1: They spoke well to him: the Rabbis, [who say] that they come to permit the fat of undomesticated animals and not to separate.
gershom:a10.1: Rather, this is the reason of Rabbi Yishmael, as he holds: let it write “all fat of ox” to exclude undomesticated animals, and sheep and goat would be included in “ox,” since they are domesticated animals like an ox. Then for what law did it write them? To separate.
gershom:a11.1: I would say: let us derive “ox” from Shabbat. “Ox” is written here, and regarding Shabbat it is written “your ox and your donkey”; just as with Shabbat, undomesticated animals and birds are like them, since from the superfluous “and all your animals” it was included that one may not perform labor with them on Shabbat (and there is labor with birds, such as threshing with geese and roosters),
gershom:a12.1: so too here, with eating fat, undomesticated animals and birds are like it, and their fat is forbidden.
gershom:a13.1: They spoke well to him: the Rabbis, that this is why they are needed, and not to separate.
gershom:a14.1: Rabbi Yishmael holds: if so, let the verse write “all fat of sheep” alone, and you could not derive a verbal analogy from Shabbat, since neither sheep nor goat is written there. Since it has an increase in libations: as it is written, “and their libations, half a hin for the bull.”
gershom:a15.1: What about a goat? It has an increase regarding idol worship by an individual, as it is written, “he shall offer a she-goat in its first year,” which is not so with these. An ox has an increase regarding idol worship by the community, as it is written, “all the congregation shall offer one young bull,” etc.
gershom:a16.1: For they have an aspect of increase: an ox has more libations, which are fit for the altar; a sheep’s tail is offered on the altar; which is not so with a goat.
gershom:a17.1: He spoke well to him: that they are needed, and they do not come to separate.
gershom:a18.1: Actually: as we said at the outset, that if so, that they do not come to separate, let it write, etc.
gershom:a19.1: And a matter is learned from its context: just as there are no undomesticated animals among sacrificial animals, so too there are none in the prohibition of fat.
gershom:a20.1: And “ox and sheep and goat” comes only to separate.
gershom:a21.1: By inference the Rabbis, who say they are needed, hold we do not derive a matter from its context? But that is one of the thirteen principles by which the Torah is expounded!
gershom:a22.1: Rabbi Yishmael holds we derive: the prohibition of “all fat of ox” from the prohibition of “a perpetual statute.” “A perpetual statute” is certainly written in the context of sacrificial animals, since before it and after it the passage speaks only of sacrificial animals; but “all fat of ox” is not written so fully in the context of sacrificial animals, since next to it is “and the fat of a carcass and the fat of a torn animal,” which are non-sacred. And since we derive the prohibition of “all fat” from the prohibition of “a perpetual statute,” which is written about sacrificial animals (but this “all fat of ox” is not written in the context of sacrificial animals, among which there are no undomesticated animals), even had it written “You shall eat no fat” without specification [and not] written “ox and sheep and goat,” there would be no doubt about the fat of undomesticated animals, since they are not among sacrificial animals.
gershom:a23.1: Therefore “ox and sheep and goat” is to separate: it comes for lashes, and he is liable for each and every one. [An editor’s note: it seems from this that our Rabbi had a different reading here: that the Rabbis hold we derive from the superfluous words only a mere prohibition, that he transgresses three prohibitions, but not for lashes.] A mere prohibition; but to separate the lashes [like] the karet penalties we still do not know. Rather, we derive the prohibition of “all fat” and the prohibition of “a perpetual statute” from the karet, as it is written, “For whoever eats the fat of the animal…”.
gershom:a24.1: Just as that one is to separate: to render one liable for each animal fit to be offered.
gershom:a25.1: So too this one: the prohibition of “all fat,” and “ox” of non-sacred animals, is to separate lashes and karet for each one.
gershom:a26.1: And the Rabbis: say that from the karet, from which you want to derive separate lashes, you cannot derive, since we derive a prohibition from a prohibition that resembles it, and that is “a matter learned from its context,” as it says in the chapter Kol HaBasar: “You shall not eat it, that it may be well with you”: the verse speaks of meat in milk. Or is it only about other prohibitions? You said: go out and learn from the thirteen principles: a matter learned from its context. What is the verse speaking of? “You shall not eat it” above is about two kinds, as it is written, “you shall not eat the life with the flesh”; so too here, two kinds, that is meat in milk. Evidently we derive a prohibition from a prohibition that resembles it, but we do not derive a prohibition from karet; therefore he is liable only once.
gershom:a27.1: Another version: Rabbi Yishmael holds we derive [from] the prohibition of “a perpetual statute,” written in the context of sacrificial animals, from which you cannot include the fat of undomesticated animals, since there are no undomesticated animals among sacrificial animals. And from “all fat of ox” too you cannot include the fat of undomesticated animals, for even had it been written without specifics, there would be no doubt about undomesticated animals that their fat is forbidden, since we derive this “all fat of ox” from the fat of the karet: just as with the karet it specifies a domesticated animal and not an undomesticated one, so too here. Therefore “ox and sheep and goat” is to separate.
gershom:a28.1: And the Rabbis derive a prohibition from a prohibition, etc.
gershom:a29.1: And if you wish, say [of] the Rabbis: this is the reason it does not come to separate, since they need “ox and sheep and goat” for this exposition, as Rav Mari said to Rav Zevid in the chapter Kol HaBasar: But now, since you include the tail from “all fat,” the tail of a non-sacred animal should be forbidden to eat! He said to him: Regarding you, the verse states, “You shall eat no fat of ox, or sheep, or goat”: complete fat, equal in all three, which goes up among the sacrificial portions, is forbidden, excluding the tail, which is not equal in all three, as it exists only in a sheep. That is why they are written: to permit the tail of non-sacred animals.
gershom:a30.1: And Rabbi Yishmael would say to you: if so, by your reasoning, let the verse say “all fat of ox and sheep,” fat equal in both of them, and the tail is not equal in both. For what did it write goat? To separate.
gershom:a31.1: And the Rabbis: say that since it wrote ox and sheep, it wrote goat as well.
gershom:a32.1: Rabbi Yishmael concedes: even though [he derives from a verse] to render one liable for each one, that applies to lashes; but regarding an offering he brings only one sin offering, since this prohibition, written for all three together, does not resemble the prohibition of forbidden relations, where a prohibition is written for each and every forbidden relative.
gershom:a33.1: “And does one” and “and does them”: that is, one that is them [several].
gershom:a34.1: To render one liable for each and every one, that if he ate fat and fat of one name: that is, two olive-bulks of fat of one species in two lapses of awareness, he is liable to two; or two names, such as an olive-bulk of the fat on the innards and an olive-bulk from upon the intestines, or an olive-bulk of ox fat and an olive-bulk of sheep fat, in one lapse of awareness, he is liable to two.
gershom:a35.1: But two names in one lapse of awareness, why is he liable to two? There is neither a division of lapses nor a division of prohibitions, since with non-sacred animals there is only one, “all fat of ox, or sheep, or goat.” [Rav Ḥisda answers:] for example, where he ate fat of notar, where there are two prohibitions.
gershom:a36.1: If so, let him be liable on account of the sacred as well: since of notar it is written, “No non-priest shall eat of the sacred,” for even a priest is a non-priest with regard to notar; and that makes three prohibitions.
gershom:a37.1: Fat of a carcass: he is flogged two, one on account of fat and one on account of a carcass.
gershom:a38.1: Fat of consecrated animals: he is flogged two, one on account of fat and one on account of the sacred. And even though two prohibitions are written about fat, the Rabbis hold that the prohibition of “all fat of ox” speaks of non-sacred animals and not of sacrificial ones.
gershom:a39.1: And Rabbi Yehuda says: for fat of consecrated animals he is flogged three, since he holds that both prohibitions are written about the sacred, and he is liable to three. Rav Sheshet could have answered in accordance with the Rabbis, who say he is liable to two for the fat of sacrificial animals; but he established it according to Rabbi Yehuda because it teaches us a novelty: that Rabbi Yehuda renders one liable for fat twice on account of two prohibitions, and that is “two names in one lapse of awareness.”
gershom:a40.1: If so, if you speak of a novelty, let us establish it according to Rabbi Yishmael, who says that for fat he is flogged three; and where he ate two names he is flogged two. Rather, why did he not establish it, etc.
rashi:b1.1: Regarding an offering: and the baraita above speaks of an offering, since regarding sin offerings it is written, “and does from one of them.”
rashi:b2.1: What are we dealing with here: that which it teaches, “two names,” is where he ate them in two dishes, two foods, which are two names, such as a stew and a roast.
rashi:b2.2: (Another version: he is liable to two, one on account of fat and one on account of the sacred, the guilt offering for misuse; and not like Rabbi Yehuda, who renders one liable twice on account of fat, on account of two prohibitions written about fat in two verses.)
rashi:b2.3: Of Rabbi Yehoshua: in the chapter Amru Lo (below, Keritot 15b).
rashi:b4.1: Two verses: one about sacrificial animals, “a perpetual statute,” and one [applying] both to non-sacred and to sacrificial animals. Therefore with the fat of consecrated animals there are two prohibitions on account of fat. And Rabbi Yehuda derives the fat of non-sacred animals as we say in the chapter Elu Overin (Pesaḥim 43b): “For whoever eats the fat of the animal”: I have only the fat of unblemished animals, fit to be offered; the fat of blemished animals, from where? The verse states “whoever.” Non-sacred animals, from where? The verse states “for whoever.”
rashi:b5.1: The Rabbis hold the prohibition of “a perpetual statute” is about sacrificial animals: since it is written in the context of sacrificial animals; and the prohibition of “all fat” is about non-sacred animals and not sacrificial ones.
rashi:b6.1: This is the reading: “But non-sacred animals, whose fat is forbidden, say not.” Its explanation: but non-sacred animals, which are lenient, say their fat is not forbidden. “Whose fat is forbidden, say not” means: say its fat is not forbidden. It is an inverted expression, a turn of phrase of the Jerusalem reading.
rashi:b7.1: Fat of consecrated animals was permitted from its general prohibition: since the tail is called fat in a sheep, and it was permitted in an ox and a goat.
rashi:b8.1: And Rabbi Yehuda holds that when it is written, etc.: as we said above.
rashi:b9.1: By inference the Rabbis do not derive: [said] in astonishment.
rashi:b10.1: We derive a prohibition from a prohibition and a prohibition from karet: a matter from its context; whether a prohibition from a prohibition, as elsewhere with a limb from a living animal in the chapter (Kol HaBasar) (Ḥullin 102a), or a prohibition from karet, as here: just as the karet is about sacrificial animals, so too the prohibition is about sacrificial animals.
rashi:b10.2: And the Rabbis hold it is a prohibition from a prohibition that we derive: as there; but a prohibition from karet we do not derive. Therefore it is written about non-sacred animals. In this too the books are corrupt, and the whole [longer] reading does not belong.
rashi:b11.1: This is the reading: The Sages taught: “All fat and all blood you shall not eat.” Rabbi Yehuda says: Just as for fat he is flogged two, so too for blood he is flogged two. And the Rabbis say: There is only one warning in it.
rashi:b12.1: What is different about fat: that is, why did it write blood together with fat? Let it write it on its own, and I would know he is flogged two. For what is different about fat, that he is flogged two without the juxtaposition? That is, blood too has two verses written, if it were written on its own, such as “You shall eat no blood”; why does it need to be written in “a perpetual statute” together with fat?
rashi:b15.1: Blood is excluded from misuse, at the end of Kol HaBasar in Sheḥitat Ḥullin (117b). One might say: just as it was excluded from the guilt offering for misuse, so too it is excluded from lashes for a non-priest [eating it]. It teaches us [otherwise]. [Rashi reads “misuse” where the daf has “ritual impurity.”]
rashi:b15.2: This is the reading: “It might enter your mind to say: since it was excluded from misuse, it is also excluded from [the prohibition of] a non-priest; it teaches us [otherwise].”
rashi:b16.1: But according to the Rabbis: since we answered that according to Rabbi Yehuda the juxtaposition is needed only on account of [the prohibition of] a non-priest, and the Rabbis disagree with him and say there is only one warning in it, by inference they hold it is excluded from [the prohibition of] a non-priest as well. So according to them, why do I need the juxtaposition?
rashi:b17.1: Just as fat is unique in that its fat is distinct from its flesh: since the prohibition of fat is stated only for ox, sheep and goat, whose fat is forbidden and whose flesh is permitted.
rashi:b17.2: And they do not combine with each other: for its prohibition, since there is only the prohibition of fat by itself here, and the permitted does not combine with the forbidden, except with the prohibitions of a nazirite.
rashi:b17.3: So too blood: even though its prohibition applies to non-kosher animals, so that the blood and the flesh would be fit to combine to make one liable for an olive-bulk of both on account of a non-kosher animal, they do not combine. For blood is learned from fat: just as with fat, its being distinct necessarily keeps it from combining, since they are distinct, one forbidden and one permitted, and the forbidden and the permitted do not combine; so too the blood of non-kosher animals, since their blood is distinct from their flesh, in that the blood carries a karet prohibition on account of blood, which is not so with the flesh, does not combine even with regard to the [prohibition of a] non-kosher [animal].
rashi:b18.1: Creeping animals are excluded: from the rule of this juxtaposition, since their blood is not distinct from their flesh, as one is not warned about their blood on account of blood but on account of a creeping animal, as we say in the chapter Dam Sheḥita (below, Keritot 21b): “Creeping animals are excluded, which have no light impurity,” etc. Therefore they combine with each other, since they have one name. Therefore the blood of a snake and its flesh combine, since one is not warned about their blood on account of blood, as we say in the chapter Dam Sheḥita (there), that the warning about blood applies only to domesticated animals, undomesticated animals and birds, etc.
rashi:b19.1: The blood of a creeping animal is derived from “And this”: for if it came to teach about the creeping animal itself, it is already written, “These are the impure for you.”
rashi:b21.1: Therefore: since you said that whatever’s blood is not distinct from its flesh combines.
rashi:b21.2: A snake too: even though it is not subject to impurity, its blood combines with its flesh for an olive-bulk for eating, since one is warned about its blood only on account of its flesh.
rashi:b21.3: Which were included for impurity: as we said, “And this is impure for you” taught that the blood of a creeping animal and its flesh combine for impurity.
rashi:b22.1: Three karet penalties: two in [the portion of] Aḥarei Mot and one in Tzav et Aharon.
rashi:b24.1: And even according to Rabbi Yehuda: he does not derive the blood of exudate from one of these karet penalties.
rashi:b25.2: What does the verse teach with “any blood”: in Aḥarei Mot: “Any man of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who sojourn among them, who eats any blood, I will set My face…”. I have [karet] only for the blood of sacrificial animals with which the soul goes out, through which atonement is achieved, which is fit for atonement on the altar, since atonement is written here, “and I have given it to you upon the altar to atone,” and these are the ones fit for atonement.
rashi:b26.1: Blood of non-sacred animals and blood of exudate: of sacrificial animals, which are not fit for atonement, as we say at the end of Tamid Nishḥat in Pesaḥim (65a).
rashi:b27.1: Rather: in fact [this is according to] the Rabbis, who do not derive non-sacred blood from the inclusive word “any.” Even though they do not hold there is karet for the blood of exudate, they need one karet for the blood of covering: the blood of an undomesticated animal or bird that one covered and it became uncovered. It might enter your mind to say it was nullified to the ground, and if he then ate it, it is mere dust and he should not be liable. It teaches us [otherwise].
rashi:b28.1: Five prohibitions: those that do not come for another exposition: one (Leviticus 3:17), “a perpetual statute”; one in Tzav et Aharon (Leviticus 7[:26]), “And you shall eat no manner of blood in any of your dwellings”; one in Aḥarei Mot (Leviticus 17[:14]), “You shall not eat the blood of any flesh”; and one in Re’eh (Deuteronomy 12:16), “You shall not eat it; you shall pour it out upon the earth like water.” That makes five. And that which is written before it, “You shall not eat the life with the flesh,” speaks of a limb from a living animal; and that which is written after it, “You shall not eat it,” we establish in the chapter Kol HaBasar in Sheḥitat Ḥullin (115b) as a warning against meat in milk. It is also written in Re’eh, “Only you shall not eat its blood,” which we establish in the second chapter of Bekhorot (15a) as about the milk of disqualified consecrated animals. And what is written in Aḥarei Mot, “No soul of you shall eat blood,” Torat Kohanim establishes as warning adults concerning minors.
rashi:b29.1: Rabbi Illa said: one who ate [second] tithe of grain, wine and oil is flogged three: on account of “You may not eat within your gates…”.
rashi:b31.1: With a positive mitzva: a prohibition that comes by inference from a positive mitzva is [treated as] a positive mitzva.
tosafot:b1.1: Rabbi Yehuda concedes regarding an offering: even though it said above that wherever there are two prohibitions and one karet, the sin offerings are divided between them, that is only with two acts, such as smearing and compounding [the anointing oil]; but with one act he did not say there is a division.
tosafot:b12.1: Blood too should be flogged three: This is puzzling: why does he need to say this with the prohibition of a non-priest? Even without it one finds three for it: one is written about it explicitly, “And you shall eat no manner of blood in any of your dwellings,” and from the juxtaposition there are two more, “just as fat is flogged two, so too blood,” etc. If so, there are three without the prohibition of a non-priest.
tosafot:b20.1: That applies to impurity: which is stringent, as its measure is a lentil-bulk; but with eating, which is an olive-bulk, say not. This is puzzling: let us state the juxtaposition and do without “And this is impure for you,” and derive impurity from eating.
tosafot:b27.1: Rather, say one for non-sacred blood: and according to Rabbi Yehuda too: one for sacrificial blood and the blood of exudate, one for the blood of non-sacred animals, and one for the blood of covering. And the baraita that teaches “the blood of non-sacred animals and the blood of exudate, from where?” is not meant precisely, as though both came from the one verse “any.”
tosafot:b27.2: For the blood of covering: the verse was needed so that we not say [from] “You shall not eat it; you shall pour it out upon the earth like water,” which implies that what is not poured out, one is not liable for. It teaches us [otherwise].
gershom:b1.1: [A printer’s note: “Up to here belongs to 4a.”] Now too it cannot be established according to Rabbi Yehuda, since he said, etc. What novelty does the baraita teach us, that he is liable to two?
gershom:b2.1: Reish Lakish said: This is what it teaches us: for example, where he ate two olive-bulks of fat of non-sacred animals in two dishes, that is, in two cooked foods, one roasted and one boiled, and these are two names. That is why he is liable to two, according to Rabbi Yehoshua, who said in this tractate, in the chapter Amru Lo: Rabbi Yehoshua said: I heard that one who eats from one offering in five dishes in one lapse of awareness is liable for each and every one on account of misuse; he holds that dishes separate.
gershom:b3.1: Another version: for example, where he ate fat of consecrated property, and it teaches us a novelty: that he is liable to two, not like Rabbi Yehuda, who says three.
gershom:b4.1: They laughed at it: if it teaches us a novelty, let us establish it as where he ate fat of ox, sheep and goat, and it is Rabbi Yishmael, who says he is flogged three; and what it teaches, “liable to two,” is where he ate only two, of ox and sheep. Rather, why did he not establish it, etc.? Since he concedes that he is liable to only one sin offering for fat. Now too, according to Rabbi Yehuda, etc. Rather, certainly one on account of fat and one on account of the sacred. And now too the baraita can be established according to Rabbi Yehuda, and both according to the Rabbis and according to Rabbi Yishmael; what novelty does it teach us?
gershom:b5.1: Rather, Reish Lakish said: that the baraita deals with this, for example where he ate them in two dishes, and it is Rabbi Yehoshua.
gershom:b6.1: Granted according to Rabbi Yehuda: this is why two verses are written about fat, and he holds both are written about sacrificial animals. But the Rabbis hold one speaks of non-sacred animals and not of sacrificial ones; therefore he is flogged only two, one on account of fat and one on account of the sacred.
gershom:b7.1: And they are necessary: one for non-sacred animals, one for sacrificial animals.
gershom:b8.1: For had it written about sacrificial animals: I would say non-sacred animals are not derived from it, since the reason fat is forbidden with sacrificial animals is that they are stringent, being forbidden to non-priests; therefore their fat is forbidden and one is liable for it. But the fat of non-sacred animals, which are not stringent, say it carries a mere prohibition but one is not liable to a sin offering. That is why it wrote “all fat of ox,” etc., that with non-sacred animals too he is liable.
gershom:b9.1: And had it written: about non-sacred animals and not about sacrificial ones, I would say it is the fat of non-sacred animals that is forbidden, since it was not permitted from its general prohibition, neither for the Most High nor for an ordinary person. But the fat of sacrificial animals, which was permitted from its general prohibition for the Most High after the sprinkling, and whose meat too was permitted from its general prohibition after the sprinkling, say: since their meat was permitted, their fat was permitted. It is necessary [to teach] that it is forbidden.
gershom:b10.1: And my teacher told us there are books in which it is written thus: “I would say it is non-sacred animals whose fat is forbidden, since it was not permitted from its general prohibition”; that is, non-sacred animals have no permission out of a general prohibition, since they are always permitted. “But the fat of consecrated animals, which were permitted from their general prohibition,” since the meat itself is forbidden before the sprinkling and permitted after the sprinkling, “I would say: since its meat was permitted from its general prohibition,” etc.
gershom:b11.1: And Rabbi Yehuda holds that when it is written: “all fat of ox” is written in the context of sacrificial animals, since it speaks of sacrificial animals above, and a matter is learned from its context. But then, by inference, the Rabbis do not hold “a matter is learned from its context”? Rather, in general everyone holds a matter is learned from its context, and here they disagree about this: Rabbi Yehuda holds we derive the prohibition of “all fat of ox” from the prohibition of “a perpetual statute,” and that prohibition from the karet, which speaks of a sacrificial animal; and just as the karet is to separate for each and every animal, so too these prohibitions are to separate. Therefore he is flogged three.
gershom:b12.1: And the Rabbis hold: “all fat of ox” is written about non-sacred animals, and we derive a prohibition from a prohibition for a mere prohibition, as it said above, that this is “a matter learned from its context,” since one prohibition resembles the other; a prohibition from karet we do not derive, since it does not resemble it. Therefore you cannot derive from it to separate, and he is flogged only two. And Rabbi Yehuda, who establishes both verses about sacrificial animals, includes the fat of non-sacred animals from “all fat of ox,” for we have heard that Rabbi Yehuda expounds “all” in tractate Zevaḥim. And both the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda derive karet for the fat of non-sacred animals from the inclusion in “For whoever eats fat,” for even one who does not expound “all” expounds “for all.”
gershom:b13.1: But according to Rabbi Yehuda, who establishes both about sacrificial animals, [in] “all fat and all blood,” what does “all blood” come for? It was written here to tell you: just as for fat of sacrificial animals he is flogged two, so too for blood he is flogged two. That is why it juxtaposed it to fat.
gershom:b14.1: What is different about fat: that it is obvious to him that he is flogged two without a juxtaposition; that is, it needs no juxtaposition, because two verses are written about it, etc.
gershom:b15.1: Rather, say: this is why the juxtaposition comes, for it might enter your mind: since it was excluded from impurity, as we learn at the end of Kol HaBasar, “Why do I need three verses about blood? ‘To you… to atone’: one to exclude it from notar, one to exclude it from misuse and one to exclude it from impurity,” it is also excluded from the prohibition of a non-priest.
gershom:b16.1: But according to the Rabbis: who hold he is flogged only once, on account of fat [so the text; the subject is blood], what does the juxtaposition come for?
gershom:b17.1: For that which is taught, which says: just as fat is unique in that its fat is distinct from its flesh, the fat forbidden and the flesh permitted, and they do not combine with each other, so that if he ate half an olive-bulk of fat and half an olive-bulk of meat they do not combine (for with all the prohibitions in the Torah the permitted does not combine with the forbidden, and even with sacrificial animals the permitted does not combine with the forbidden, as Rabbi Yehoshua taught: With all the offerings in the Torah, if an olive-bulk of meat or an olive-bulk of fat remained of them, he sprinkles the blood; half an olive-bulk of meat and half an olive-bulk of fat, he does not sprinkle the blood), so too whatever’s blood is distinct from its flesh does not combine, and he is not liable. I will exclude the blood of creeping animals, whose blood is not distinct from their flesh, since both are forbidden to eat, and they combine with each other, as we learned in tractate Me’ila (17a): The blood of a creeping animal and its flesh combine for a lentil-bulk. And they derive from the juxtaposition that the blood of a creeping animal and its flesh combine. [An editor’s note: all this is cited in the Arukh, entry dam 3.]
gershom:b18.1: But from “and this is impure for you” it was taught about the blood of creeping animals and their flesh that they combine, since it is superfluous, as it is written, “and these are the impure for you among all the creeping animals.”
gershom:b19.1: It might enter your mind: from “and this is impure for you” one derives that it combines for impurity, but for eating, say it does not combine to make one liable to lashes. The juxtaposition teaches us that it combines.
gershom:b20.1: Another version: Granted according to Rabbi Yehuda, who expounds this verse “all fat and all blood” for the juxtaposition, well and good, as it is taught: “All fat and all blood,” etc.; and the Rabbis say there is only a warning in it, one prohibition. But according to the Rabbis, what does the juxtaposition come for? It is needed, etc.
gershom:b21.1: Ravina said: since it is so, that you said whatever’s blood is not distinct from its flesh combines, the blood of a snake and its flesh combine, even though it is not one of the eight creeping animals.
gershom:b22.1: What does he teach us: Ravina? That is the juxtaposition, for what difference is there between a creeping animal and its flesh and a snake and its flesh?
gershom:b23.1: Ravina’s statement was needed, and the juxtaposition was needed: it might enter your mind that it is the creeping animal that was included for impurity, as it is written, “and this is impure for you”; since it combines for impurity, it combines for eating. But a snake, which was not included for impurity, since it does not impart impurity, [would not]. The juxtaposition teaches us, etc.
gershom:b24.1: Three karet penalties regarding blood: why? One in the portion Tzav et Aharon and two in the portion Aḥarei Mot.
gershom:b25.1: I have only: principally the blood of sacrificial animals, with which the soul goes out, which atones, as it is written, “for it is the blood that atones by reason of the life.”
gershom:b26.1: The blood of non-sacred animals and the blood of exudate, from where? The verse states, “any blood.” The blood of non-sacred animals is not meant precisely here, since for the blood of non-sacred animals we find karet explicitly, as it is written, “who hunts,” etc. Rather, [the third is] one for the blood of covering, the blood of an undomesticated animal or bird, both according to Rabbi Yehuda and according to the Rabbis.
gershom:b27.1: Five prohibitions: written about blood: the prohibition of “a perpetual statute,” and the prohibition of “You shall eat no fat of ox, or sheep, or goat” [so the text], and three in the portion Aḥarei Mot: one for the blood of non-sacred animals, etc.; for the blood of the limbs, which comes out of the limbs when they are cut (after) [before] slaughter, which is a limb from a living animal. And there are four more prohibitions about blood, and they come for expositions: “And you shall say to them, any man,” etc., comes to warn adult Israelites concerning minors, that they keep them from blood; “Only you shall not eat its blood,” of a firstborn, we establish in Bekhorot: what is “its blood”? Its milk, of disqualified consecrated animals; “You shall not eat the life with the flesh” comes to forbid blood from a living animal, the blood of bloodletting with which the soul goes out; and “You shall not eat it; you shall pour it out upon the earth” comes for meat in milk, as it says in the chapter Kol HaBasar. One who eats second tithe of these three kinds outside, grain, wine and oil, is flogged three, because it is written, “You may not eat within your gates,” etc.
gershom:b28.1: If from that one: “And you shall eat,” I would say this applies only in that he transgresses a positive mitzva; that is, a prohibition that comes by inference from a positive mitzva is a positive mitzva.
